overview.text: Duke Power Company has applied to the Federal Power Commission for a license to build the Bad Creek Pumped Storage Project, a 1,000-megawatt hydroelectric plant in Oconee County, South Carolina that would pump water between a new 318-acre upper reservoir on Bad and West Bad Creeks and the existing 7,565-acre Lake Jocassee below. The project sits in remote, forested northwestern Oconee County near the North Carolina line, and would mainly affect trout anglers, hikers, and users of nearby state parks and national forests rather than displace residents, while adding roughly $950,000 to $1,350,000 per year in taxes to Oconee County. The Commission compared Bad Creek against denying the license, alternative pumped-storage sites (Long Spur Ridge, Bearcamp Creek, Coley Creek), other generation types (nuclear, coal, combustion turbines, conventional hydro), and conservation measures. Main environmental impacts include permanent clearing of about 505 acres of forest and wildlife habitat, inundation of 2.3 miles of trout stream in Bad and West Bad Creeks, a 53% flow reduction in Howard Creek — the only South Carolina tributary with a trout spawning run — and further loss of coldwater trout habitat in Lake Jocassee. The South Carolina Wildlife and Marine Resources Department opposed the project as proposed, Trout Unlimited and the Sierra Club raised serious objections, while the Department of the Interior, EPA (with 'environmental reservations'), and the mayor of Walhalla submitted more qualified or supportive comments.

project_description.text: Duke Power Company is seeking a federal license to build the Bad Creek Pumped Storage Project in Oconee County, South Carolina, about 8 miles north of Salem — a 1,000-MW hydroelectric plant that stores energy by pumping water uphill during off-peak hours and generating during peak demand. It would use a new 318-acre upper reservoir on Bad and West Bad Creeks (full pond elevation 2,310 feet) and the existing 7,565-acre Lake Jocassee as the lower reservoir, with four reversible 250-MW pump-turbines in an underground powerhouse connected by a 1.25-mile tunnel. Water level in the upper reservoir would swing up to 160 vertical feet in a daily operating cycle, and the plant could run at full load for 32 hours. Power would leave the site on a new 525-kV transmission line running about 18 miles south to the Oconee Nuclear Station switchyard, plus a 100-kV line to the existing Jocassee project.

affected_community.text: The project sits in a remote, rugged, and largely uninhabited stretch of northwestern Oconee County, South Carolina, near the North Carolina line, within the Horsepasture Game Management Area and the proclamation boundary of Sumter National Forest; all required lands are already owned by Duke's subsidiary Crescent Land and Timber Corporation, so no residences or businesses would be displaced. The nearest town is Salem, South Carolina (1970 population 300), about 8 miles south; the surrounding four-county area (Oconee and Pickens in SC, Jackson and Transylvania in NC) had a 1970 population of 140,990 and an economy dominated by textile and wood-products industries, with unemployment reaching 8% in Oconee and 16% in Pickens by February 1975. About 100 construction-worker families would move to nearby towns, and Oconee County would receive roughly $950,000 to $1,350,000 in taxes per year — about 25% of its 1974 property tax collections. Directly affected users include trout anglers on Howard Creek and Lake Jocassee, hikers on the Foothills Trail, and visitors to three nearby South Carolina state parks (Oconee, Table Rock, and Keowee-Toxaway), Sumter and Nantahala National Forests, and the Chattooga National Wild and Scenic River about 5 miles west.

alternatives_overview.text: The Federal Power Commission considered four broad options: denying Duke's license and forcing use of another power source, building at a different pumped-storage site, using a different generation method, or granting the license with protective conditions. Alternative generation types evaluated include conventional hydro, simple-cycle and combined-cycle combustion turbines, coal-fired steam, base-load nuclear, conservation and rate revisions, purchased power, and federal (TVA) development. From about 20 potential pumped-storage locations, three alternative sites — Long Spur Ridge, Bearcamp Creek, and Coley Creek, all using Lake Jocassee as the lower reservoir — were studied in detail. Bad Creek was found to be the lowest-cost power source available to Duke except possibly Long Spur Ridge (which Duke is holding for a future higher-capacity 2,200-MW development), and without Bad Creek Duke's reserve margin would fall well below the 18–22% range recommended by the Southern Electric Reliability Council after 1982. Purchased power was rejected because forecast 1985 reserve margins in the surrounding VACAR subregion (10.8%) and TVA are already below that recommended range, and conservation and load-management measures were set aside for lack of quantitative data and because construction lead times preclude waiting for study results.

environmental_impact.text: Construction and operation would permanently clear about 505 acres of forest and wildlife habitat and inundate roughly 2.3 miles of trout stream — about 1.0 percent of South Carolina's trout streams by length — in Bad and West Bad Creeks. Flow in Howard Creek just below its junction with Bad Creek would drop about 53%, threatening the only documented trout spawning run in the state (rainbow and brown trout out of Lake Jocassee) and rendering at least 3.5 miles of the creek unsuitable for trout during construction plus a 2–3 year recovery, with commenters estimating disruption of the spawning run for 8 to 12 years. In Lake Jocassee, combined operation of Bad Creek, the existing Jocassee pumped-storage plant, and the Oconee Nuclear Plant is expected to eliminate roughly 450,000 acre-feet of optimum coldwater trout habitat (water below 20°C with 5 mg/L dissolved oxygen) in the main body of the lake, and fish passing through the pump-turbines would suffer 56.5–65.1% mortality in pumping mode and 35.4–74.8% in generating mode. Daily 160-foot drawdowns of the upper reservoir would expose a barren mudflat strip up to about 718 feet wide. Highly erodible soils, already gullying from past logging and exploratory drilling, could push total suspended solids in construction runoff to 44,000 mg/L during a 10-year storm; Lake Jocassee largemouth bass already carry mercury above the FDA 0.5 µg/g limit (mean 3.01 µg/g in 1973–74). Rare species at risk include Oconee bells (Shortia galacifolia), on the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service proposed endangered plants list, plus Fothergilla major and loosestrife, with 26 Fothergilla and 22 loosestrife specimens transplanted by the applicant. Offsetting benefits include local tax revenue, short-term construction jobs, and a 31-mile hiking trail with shelters to replace lost recreation.

public_response.text: The draft EIS was circulated to federal, state, and local agencies plus applicant and public groups, drawing sharply divided comments. The South Carolina Wildlife and Marine Resources Department opposed the project as proposed, citing the loss of trout streams, the Howard Creek spawning run, and threats to Lake Jocassee's two-story fishery, and asked FPC to delay licensing. The Department of the Interior said it could not fully endorse the project until impacts on Lake Jocassee's two-story fishery and Howard Creek's trout fishery are mitigated. EPA Region IV rated the draft 'ER' (environmental reservations) and '2' (insufficient information). The South Carolina Chapter of Trout Unlimited objected that the DEIS missed the documented rainbow and brown trout spawning run in lower Howard Creek and requested that licensing be deferred and public meetings be held. The Joseph LeConte Chapter of the Sierra Club objected to piecemeal review of just Bad Creek rather than all contemplated pumped-storage development in the basin. In contrast, the mayor of Walhalla endorsed the project, and the Army Corps of Engineers, Forest Service, TVA, and Nuclear Regulatory Commission had no substantive objections. FPC Staff declined to defer licensing, concluding it was 'not in the best interest of the public' to wait, and noted Duke had agreed to mitigation including conveying a 375-acre parcel on Eastatoe Creek to the state.
